opus-5.5.text:
Well, it wasn't really something I set out to do. I started my blog, Shtetl-Optimized, back around 2005, mostly to write about complexity theory, quantum computing, and whatever else was on my mind. But I kept noticing that the popular articles about quantum computing almost always got the central point wrong. They'd say a quantum computer "tries every possible answer in parallel" and then just picks out the right one, which, if it were true, would mean quantum computers could solve NP-complete problems instantly. That's not how it works. The whole game is interference: you have to choreograph things so the amplitudes for the wrong answers cancel and the amplitudes for the right answer reinforce. Only for problems with very special structure, like factoring, do we know how to do that.

Then companies started appearing and making big claims, like D-Wave around 2007, announcing speedups that the evidence just didn't support. Journalists would repeat the press releases uncritically. I felt that if people who actually understood the theory stayed silent, the field would end up with a credibility problem when the promised miracles didn't arrive. So I started writing posts pointing out what was and wasn't supported, and somehow I ended up with this title of "Chief Quantum Hype Skeptic," or whatever people call me.

I should say, though, that I've never been a skeptic of quantum computing itself. I think it's one of the most exciting things in science, and the recent progress in error correction and hardware has been real. My problem is with claims that outrun the evidence. Ironically, I think honesty about what quantum computers can't do is the best thing for the field in the long run.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Aaronson began writing posts because journalists repeated unsupported claims and knowledgeable people were staying silent, but it does not say his blog became a clearinghouse or that no one else was filling that role.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention journalists asking for a one-sentence explanation or Aaronson estimating that he could explain quantum computing in about ten minutes.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it was never something I set out to do. When I started the blog back in 2005, I thought of it as a place to talk about complexity theory, quantum computing, whatever was on my mind. But what happened almost immediately was that people started sending me things. A press release would come out saying some company had built a quantum computer that would solve all of humanity's problems, or an article would claim that quantum computers work by trying every possible answer in parallel, and people would email me and say, "Scott, is this real? What do I make of this?"

And I realized that there's a kind of asymmetry. The people putting out the hype have every incentive to do it. There's money in it, there's attention in it. The people who actually know the field, mostly they're busy, they're doing research, they don't want to get into a public fight with someone's startup. So the correction just doesn't happen, or it happens in a seminar room where nobody outside hears it.

I think I came to feel, almost by default, that if I didn't say something, maybe nobody would. And I had this unusual position where I understood the technical details, but I also enjoyed writing for a general audience and I was willing to be blunt. Those don't always go together.

The thing I'd stress is that I'm not anti-quantum computing. Quite the opposite. I've spent my whole career on this. I think the actual science is extraordinary. But that's exactly why the hype bothers me. When someone tells the public that quantum computers will exponentially speed up everything, and then that doesn't materialize, the backlash doesn't land on the hype merchants. It lands on the field. So in a sense I see defending the real thing and attacking the fake version as the same job.

astra-6.text:
Well, when I started blogging, I wanted to explain what quantum computing actually says and why it’s interesting. And pretty quickly, that meant responding to claims that gave people the wrong picture—like the idea that a quantum computer simply tries every possible answer in parallel and then hands you the right one.

The difficulty is that, when you measure a quantum computer, you only get one outcome. The whole challenge is to choreograph the interference so that wrong answers cancel out and the answer you want becomes more likely. We know how to do that for certain problems. We don’t know how to do it for every hard problem.

And that distinction tends to disappear in the hype. So I came to see explaining those limits as part of explaining the subject itself. Quantum computing is exciting enough on its own. You don’t need to turn it into magic.

sol-6.1.text:
I started blogging because I wanted a place to talk about the things that interested me, and quantum computing was naturally a big part of that. But I kept seeing this enormous gap between what we actually knew and what people were being told—especially the idea that a quantum computer just tries every possible answer in parallel and instantly picks the right one.

The interesting question is precisely how you get an answer out. You have to choreograph interference so that wrong answers cancel and right answers get reinforced. And we only know how to do that for certain problems.

So I felt that explaining those limitations was part of explaining why quantum computing is exciting in the first place. You don’t need to claim that it will solve every hard problem. The things we have good reasons to think it could do are already remarkable.
